input.question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.
input.ground_truth: It will always be the donor's cells. It can be possible to wean off of antirejection drugs as your body gets used to the new organ, but if your whole liver is replaced by a donor liver, you do not have any of your own liver cells to replicate and replace the donor cells.

Question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.

response.prediction:
Okay, let's imagine you have a toy car, but it breaks, so your friend gives you a brand new toy car that works perfectly. You start playing with your friend’s toy car every day.

Now, your body is like you, and the new organ (like a heart or kidney) is like your friend’s toy car. When someone gets a new organ from a donor, the organ is put inside their body. But here’s what happens next:

The new organ is made of the donor’s cells, just like your friend’s toy car is made by your friend. At first, most of the organ’s cells are from the donor. But over time, some of your own body’s cells might move into the new organ, and some of the donor’s cells might not last forever.

However, the new organ will mostly stay made of the donor’s cells for a long, long time—maybe for many years. But it’s not forever forever, because little by little, your body tries to make the organ more like yours. Still, the organ will work as if it’s part of you!

So, the answer is: The new organ starts as the donor’s, but over time, some of your own cells might move in, but most of it will still be the donor’s for a very long time.
